An equity-ratio shortfall: why repaying debt, adding collateral and selling assets need different amounts

Compare three original balance-sheet adjustments after an asset-price decline, inspect their different denominators, and reconcile new outside cash without treating it as recovered investment performance.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Inspect three balance-sheet adjustments under one invented equity-ratio rule

Interactive planning lab

Outside cash used to reduce the loan$4,800
Outside cash held as extra collateral$8,000
Assets sold in the sale-only case$12,000

Original instantaneous balance-sheet illustration under an invented equity/assets requirement. Amounts are CAD, with no actual security, broker, jurisdictional margin schedule or eligibility calculation. The loan stays fixed during the selected asset-price move. Three mutually exclusive adjustments then target the same ratio: use outside cash to repay debt; add outside cash to collateral assets while leaving debt unchanged; or sell original assets and apply all proceeds to debt. The separate held-cash case is an assumed collateral arrangement, not a claim that a broker will permit cash to remain without netting the loan. If a firm applies a deposit against debt, the repayment case describes that accounting. A sale-only repair of a remaining funded account is unavailable when equity is zero or negative. No deadline, actual margin call, tax, fees, interest, further price move or lender approval is modeled. Adding outside cash is new funding, not recovered investment performance. Every displayed adjustment preserves the same pre-adjustment investment equity after subtracting its new outside funding.

The central idea

An equity ratio can improve by changing debt, assets or both. The amount required depends on which balances change, while new funding does not reverse the investment loss.

01

Identify the assets, debt and equity before calculating a shortfall

A collateral ratio combines two balances. In this illustration, equity equals the value of assets in the account minus the loan, and the required ratio is equity divided by total collateral assets. Changing either assets or debt can therefore change the ratio.

The SEC’s margin-account bulletin explains borrowing against an investment account and the possibility of demands for additional resources or asset sales. Its margin-call glossary also notes that a firm can change its threshold. These US investor-education sources provide general context, not the requirement used here.

The entered equity requirement is deliberately hypothetical. Real arrangements can apply different collateral eligibility, haircuts, cash-netting rules and rights of sale. This tool compares arithmetic under one simplified rule; it does not determine a regulatory requirement or recommend a response to a real lender.

02

Trace the default decline before adding any new money

The account begins with CAD 60,000 of assets, financed by CAD 30,000 of borrowing and CAD 30,000 of investor capital. After a 30% asset-price decline, the assets are worth CAD 42,000. The loan stays at CAD 30,000, leaving CAD 12,000 of equity.

The asset lost CAD 18,000, while the investor’s initial CAD 30,000 of equity fell by 60%. Interest and costs are excluded from this instantaneous example. The resulting equity-to-assets ratio is CAD 12,000 divided by CAD 42,000, or about 28.57%, below the invented 40% requirement.

Under that fixed loan and ratio, the boundary asset value is loan ÷ (1 − required ratio). Here it is CAD 50,000, corresponding to a decline of about 16.67% from the original CAD 60,000. This boundary comes from the selected equation. It is not a quotation of a brokerage firm’s actual trigger price.

03

Distinguish cash that reduces debt from cash that increases collateral assets

If new outside cash is used directly to repay the loan, the asset denominator stays at CAD 42,000. Equity must reach 40% of that amount, or CAD 16,800. A CAD 4,800 repayment reduces the loan to CAD 25,200 and produces that equity amount.

The separate held-cash illustration assumes new cash is added to collateral assets while the loan remains unchanged. The cash increases both assets and equity. Solving (equity + cash) ÷ (assets + cash) = required ratio gives CAD 8,000. Assets become CAD 50,000, debt stays CAD 30,000 and equity becomes CAD 20,000, again 40%.

Those are different accounting treatments. A firm may apply a cash deposit against its debit balance instead of allowing the assumed held-cash arrangement. In that situation, use the repayment treatment. Adding a deposit to assets while also subtracting the same money from debt would count one contribution twice. The model does not establish which treatment an actual agreement permits.

04

A sale followed by loan repayment reduces both sides of the ratio

In the sale-only case, assets are sold at their current assumed value and every dollar of proceeds repays the loan. A CAD 12,000 sale reduces assets from CAD 42,000 to CAD 30,000 and the loan from CAD 30,000 to CAD 18,000.

Equity remains CAD 12,000. Dividing it by the smaller CAD 30,000 asset balance gives 40%. The sale repairs the ratio without new outside cash in this example, but it does not recover the CAD 18,000 price loss. It also leaves less of the original investment inside the account. The sale proceeds are assigned to the loan, rather than becoming money for household bills.

A sale alone cannot restore a positive ratio in a remaining funded account when equity is zero or negative. For example, assets of CAD 24,000 against a CAD 30,000 loan leave negative CAD 6,000 of equity. Selling all assets still leaves CAD 6,000 of debt. The tool marks that sale-only repair unavailable; closing an empty, exactly settled account is also different from restoring a positive equity ratio.

05

Subtract new outside funding before describing the remaining investment equity

The three default adjustments show different account-equity amounts: CAD 16,800 after loan repayment, CAD 20,000 after adding held cash, and CAD 12,000 after the sale. Comparing those figures without their funding sources would favor whichever account received the most new money.

Subtract the CAD 4,800 outside repayment from the first amount and the CAD 8,000 outside cash contribution from the second. Each leaves CAD 12,000, matching the sale case, which received no new cash. The signed-bar chart performs that reconciliation and keeps the original CAD 30,000 investor capital beside it.

This is an accounting identity under unchanged execution prices, rather than a full household wealth forecast. Tax, transaction costs and subsequent price movements would create additional changes. Outside money may also have an existing purpose elsewhere in the household plan. Improving a ratio by transferring that money does not make its previous obligation disappear or establish that the investment has earned back its loss.

06

Use the profile and matrix to inspect the assumed rule

The ratio profile holds the original loan fixed while changing the asset-price move. Negative ratios indicate debt greater than asset value. The horizontal requirement is another assumption, so moving it changes the illustrated shortfall without changing what the investment is worth.

The matrix reports only outside cash applied to debt repayment. Its rows replace the asset-price decline and its columns replace the required equity ratio. The other two treatments require their own equations, which is why the matrix is not labelled simply “the margin-call amount.” Zero means no adjustment is needed for that particular assumed rule at that point.

An actual lender can have different eligible collateral, requirements, deadlines and execution rights. A favorable calculation here does not secure time to act or guarantee that a selected sale is available. Keep the three questions distinct: what the account currently owns and owes, which balances a proposed adjustment changes, and what the actual agreement requires. The charts make the first two inspectable while leaving the third to current contractual evidence.
